extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in linguistics/pragmatics, conversation analysis, and humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: Developing or evaluating accounts of humor as it occurs in everyday conversational interaction, including joke-telling, teasing, irony, and anecdote performance, with attention to timing, identity, gender, power, and multimodal cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include interactional exploitation and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Any complete theory of humor must include its exploitation in and effects on interaction, taking into account such matters as gender, power, solidarity, politeness and identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorizing humor should go beyond a purely pragmatic description of jokes and joking and explicitly analyze how humor is used and what effects it has within interactional contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real interactional data (not only joke texts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The data for an interactional analysis of humor can not be limited to joke texts in books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and analyze recordings and transcriptions of natural talk-in-interaction rather than relying solely on canned joke texts; interactional competence includes performance and response patterns observable in real conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model humor competence as performance + reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor competence must include knowing how to perform and how to receive and respond to humor and jokes, and this will encompass an account of timing for both the tellers and recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should treat both the teller's production and the recipient's responses (including timing) as integral components of humor competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ conversation/discourse/interactional methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of analysis developed in Conversation Analysis, discourse analysis and interactional sociolinguistics allowed for the detailed examination of talk-in-interaction, and this enabled the description of humorous activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fine-grained analytic tools from these methodological traditions to examine turn-taking, repair, sequencing, and other interactional structures in humorous episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat joking as a strategic social resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Research has shown how joking can work as a strategy for enhancing intimacy, but also for controlling a conversation; an account highlights the interactional achievement of puns, irony and sarcasm along with personal anecdotes and joke-telling between participants and the mutual construction of identity they accomplish in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should identify the strategic functions of humor (e.g., bonding, controlling topic/membership, identity work) and show how forms of humor accomplish these social aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for teasing and sarcasm's dual force
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversational joking – especially teasing and sarcasm – has a dual force: because it plays on relational identity, teasing directed at intimates can have the potential to hurt, even as it ratifies the bond between the interactants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate risk and solidarity effects: consider relational positioning and potential for harm versus bond-affirmation when interpreting or producing teasing and sarcastic moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider gender and power differences in deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be characterized as a gendered discourse resource on which both men and women regularly draw when negotiating their gender identities in interaction; Women and men deploy humor differently, just as those with more power or control in a particular interaction use humor differently than those who are one down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how gender and relative power shape the forms, targets, and functions of humorous behavior; note documented differences in self-targeted humor and story types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model joke performance as storytelling with laughter expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The performance of a joke follows the pattern for storytelling generally; the major difference consists in the expectation of laughter at the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply narrative structure analysis to jokes but include the specific normative expectation (and management) of recipient laughter as a distinguishing feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat jokes as 'understanding tests' requiring background knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are told as ‘understanding tests’, since not everyone necessarily gets every joke, and getting jokes involves background knowledge and rational processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses and production should consider cognitive and cultural prerequisites for 'getting' a joke and the role of jokes in testing and establishing common ground rather than merely embarrassing hearers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify functions: directing aggression and enhancing rapport
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes allow group members to direct aggression at a third party, they can help create and enhance feelings of rapport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humorous episodes, note how humor reallocates or displaces aggression and how it builds or modifies social bonds and group cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze timing as interactional coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The conversational joke performance represents a particularly salient example of interaction between the teller and the listeners. Timing in the performance of a joke is compounded of elements depending upon both the teller and the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how teller and recipient jointly manage timing (pauses, overlaps, latencies) and how timing choices affect joke uptake and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to standard prefaces, syntactic and discourse patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: There are standard joke prefaces, characteristic patterns of syntax and discourse organization in the areas of tempo, fluency and information flow, and customary reactions at the completion of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and analyze formulaic prefaces, syntactic choices, pacing, and typical post-punchline responses as features shaping joke performance and interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize anticipatory and in-performance laughter points
rubrics_metrics.description: There are characteristic points where a teller and/or a listener may laugh before the punch line: both tellers and recipients of jokes sometimes laugh about problems in the telling of a joke, and listeners may laugh in response to the preface of a joke, and at various incongruities during the performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for non-final laughter (anticipatory, reactive) in analyses and when timing joke delivery; such laughter can signal comprehension, repair, or endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use timing features as performance and reception cues
rubrics_metrics.description: All these features of joke-telling affect the overall timing of the performance: they guide the teller in how to construct and pace the performance, and they act as cues to the recipients of the joke, helping them respond to the performance in appropriate ways and to get the joke, so that they can laugh (or perhaps withhold laughter) at the right time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret timing features as both production strategies and interpretive cues; consider how pacing and cueing facilitate or hinder appropriate recipient responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage personal anecdotes to ratify identity and invite participation
rubrics_metrics.description: In exchanging anecdotes about our personal lives, we present personal identities for ratification by the other participants in the conversation. Personal anecdotes present an amusing scene which invites listeners to laugh and offer comments of their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat humorous personal narratives as interactional devices for identity work and as invitations to collaborative response; examine how details and dialogue invite co-participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow and analyze co-narration/collaborative narration where humorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative narration, whereby two or more participants contribute to or comment on a story in progress, is common; co-narration is acceptable whenever it creates humor. Collaborative narration serves to ratify group membership and modulate rapport in multiple ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document instances of co-narration, how participants coordinate additions, and how collaborative retelling functions to re-live shared experiences, confirm bonds, produce belonging, and solidify shared stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess tellability as a function of narrative dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The tellability of familiar stories hinges not on their content as such, but on the dynamics of the narrative event itself, and humor makes communal retelling desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a story is 'tellable', focus on interactional dynamics (timing, reception, co-participation) rather than mere novelty of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-verbal and multimodal aspects of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-verbal humor and joke performance (e.g., gestures, facial expressions, prosody) are components of conversational humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses and productions should incorporate multimodal cues (nonverbal behavior, prosodic contours) because they materially affect timing, comprehension, and the social functions of humor.
